routes.description: Establish consciousness as the sole immediate ontological datum, reject nonconscious emergence as an explanation of experience, and show that a universal mental foundation can preserve objective structure, causal order, and scientific tractability.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if consciousness is shown to require no reduction to a nonexperiential substrate, while the proposed consciousness-first ontology accounts for observer-independent reality, differentiated subjects, regular causation, and nonspatiotemporal structure.

motionBridge.description: Connect the irreducibility of experience and the explanatory adequacy of universal subjectivity to the conclusion that consciousness is reality's ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: Show why descriptions of nonconscious physical quantities cannot entail experiential qualities and why positing strong emergence does not close that explanatory gap.
Explain how an external mental reality can remain observer-independent and appear as a stable physical world through perceptual representation and dissociative boundaries.
Ground causal power, differentiation, and natural regularities in the intrinsic dispositions and excitation modes of universal subjectivity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the constructed narrative self from consciousness itself so that rejecting a persistent personal agent does not eliminate experience.
Account for structure beyond fundamental spacetime through meaning-bearing cognitive or semantic relations.

routes.description: Separate rejection of materialist emergence from acceptance of idealism, develop a representation-based neutral monism, and require any consciousness-first ontology to explain structured order, boundaries, causal differentiation, and phenomenal character.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a neutral representational basis can accommodate phenomenal character without treating consciousness as universal substance, while idealism's mental-substrate designation leaves indispensable explanatory work unresolved.

motionBridge.description: Connect the sufficiency of neutral monism and the unresolved explanatory commitments of idealism to denial that consciousness must be reality's ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that rejecting matter-to-consciousness emergence does not by itself select analytic idealism over other nonmaterialist ontologies.
Locate phenomenal character in representations without requiring a separate physical organism, unified self, or universal conscious substance.
Require an account of how a designated mental substrate produces boundaries, predictive representations, structured order, and differentiated causal relations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether information integration supplies an explanatory connection to subjective experience rather than only an empirical correlation.
Use experiences lacking ordinary selfhood, space, or time to examine which features an adequate fundamental ontology must explain.

sections.title: Ontological Starting Point and the Emergence Gap
sections.rationale: This issue tests the principal inference from consciousness as an immediate datum and the explanatory gap of strong emergence to a consciousness-first ontology, including whether that inference excludes neutral alternatives.

sections.title: Objective Reality, Boundaries, and Natural Order
sections.rationale: A viable route must explain how observer-independent structure, perceptual representation, embodied boundaries, evolution, and stable causal regularities arise under its proposed ontology.

sections.title: Representation, Self-Models, and Phenomenal Character
sections.rationale: The dispute over whether phenomenal character belongs to representations, consciousness itself, or a persistent subject bears directly on whether neutral monism suffices or idealism is required.

sections.title: Integrated Information and Causal Existence
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether information integration merely predicts reports or supports claims about subjective viewpoints, self-existing complexes, and the location of causal power.

sections.title: Universal Subjectivity, Differentiation, and Nonspatiotemporal Structure
sections.rationale: The proposed universal subject must account for differentiated experiences and causal order without relying on a personal self, while also explaining structure when ordinary space and time are not fundamental.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Consciousness is the sole pre-theoretical given, so ontological parsimony favors reducing nature's complexity to consciousness rather than to a postulated nonexperiential substrate.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Bernardo by name, after which the uninterrupted first-person answer states his reductionist case.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the route's initial parsimony argument and therefore has no earlier opposing locked move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly performs its constructive role by stating the foundational datum and proposed reduction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reductionist proposal, its contrast class, and its conditional parsimony claim are recoverable and consistently framed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The preference is qualified by repeated conditional language, though pre-theoretical givenness alone only partly warrants ontological priority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parsimony inference is intelligible, but it leaves a material bridge from epistemic immediacy to ontological reduction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The immediate availability of consciousness supports the premise, while the superiority of this reduction remains largely argued rather than demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level bridge by identifying consciousness as the proposed ontological foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances its positive starting point without materially interpreting a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls consciousness the one pre-theoretical given and presents reducing nature's complexity to it as the preferred ultimate reduction.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Physical quantities do not entail experiential qualities, making strong emergence explanatorily empty; idealism is preferable if it can also preserve an objective, predictable world open to science.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer explicitly responds to the moderator's emergence alternative and continues in Kastrup's established speaking turn.

response.rationale: This constructive move develops the central emergence objection and states the adequacy conditions idealism must meet, with no earlier opposing locked target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It sharply develops the central route while expressly acknowledging objective-world and scientific-adequacy requirements.

precisionFindings.rationale: The entailment objection and the conditional preference for idealism are distinct, stable, and explicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The force is appropriately limited by the express condition that idealism must preserve objectivity, prediction, and science.

charity.alternative: Strong emergence may be a legitimate primitive psychophysical law rather than a deductive entailment from physical quantities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling emergence primitive preserves logical possibility but does not supply the requested explanatory derivation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explanatory-gap inference is strong and the conditional adequacy requirement prevents a simple false-dilemma conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The quantity-quality contrast supports the criticism, though the excerpt does not compare every rival nonmaterialist ontology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the indispensable central bridge concerning why physical quantities do not explain experiential qualities.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument recognizes emergence as an available position and targets its explanatory limitation without treating it as incoherent.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts physical parameters with experiential qualities and makes idealism preferable only if it explains an external predictable world and science.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Rejecting matter-to-consciousness emergence does not establish analytic idealism, because the dissociation analogy still leaves the observed structure and order of the world unexplained.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the discussion to Susan, and the ensuing first-person critique directly names Bernardo and analytic idealism.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether failure of physical emergence selects idealism while preserving an explained objective order.
The parsimony move must justify why epistemic givenness establishes a uniquely mental ontology.

response.rationale: The reply accepts the emergence problem but denies that it uniquely establishes analytic idealism and presses the unresolved explanation of worldly structure and order.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both central inferences, but its selected evidence develops the emergence criticism more clearly than the idealism-specific underdetermination.

precisionFindings.rationale: The underdetermination challenge is recoverable, though the range of viable alternative ontologies remains only implicitly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents underdetermination as a serious problem rather than claiming a conclusive refutation of every form of idealism.

charity.alternative: Idealism is offered conditionally as the best explanation, not as a deduction solely from rejecting physical emergence.
charity.decisiveQualification: A conditional inference to the best explanation still requires comparison with neutral or other nonmaterialist alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Rejecting emergence plainly does not entail idealism, and the demand for additional explanation follows without contradiction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual underdetermination is well supported, but the excerpt gives limited affirmative development of the rival possibilities.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con route's central underdetermination bridge and challenges the pro route's main selection inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge preserves the conditional character of the pro case while correctly demanding the missing comparative step.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked proposition and span reject matter-to-consciousness emergence while maintaining that analytic idealism still owes an account of observed order.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Analytic idealism allows observer-independent external mental states that are not directly accessible but are represented through perception as the physical world.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo accepts the request to clarify his view and develops a sustained first-person account of analytic idealism.

components.text: The decisive demand is to show how idealism can retain an observer-independent, structured external world.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes personal subjectivity from external mental states and explains physical perception as representation of an inaccessible mental world.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the objectivity objection, although it does not yet fully explain the world's detailed structure and order.

precisionFindings.rationale: Externality, mentality, indirect access, and perceptual representation are clearly distinguished throughout the stated account.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims that idealism allows objective externality and states the access limitation without overstating a complete causal explanation.

charity.alternative: Objectivity may require mind-independent physical substance rather than merely states external to individual observers.
charity.decisiveQualification: Observer independence does not logically require nonmental substance, though mental structure still needs explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between individual minds, external mental states, and perceptual appearances is explicit and internally consistent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The model establishes conceptual compatibility with objectivity, but supplies limited independent evidence for the external substrate's mental character.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the indispensable central objectivity bridge by explaining observer independence and perceptual representation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response isolates the strongest objectivity concern and answers its substance assumption while retaining the structural explanatory burden.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the external world would exist without us, consists of inaccessible mental states, and appears physically through perceptual representation.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Calling an inaccessible substrate mental adds no explanatory content unless the view accounts for the machinery, boundaries, and structured predictive representations through which the world appears.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker immediately challenges the preceding explanation in second person and invokes Blackmore's own interest in predictive processing.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether labeling the inaccessible external substrate mental explains representation, machinery, and boundaries.

response.rationale: The reply directly asks where representations and predictive machinery come from and argues that the mental designation alone has not supplied those mechanisms.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly targets the explanatory gap left by the immediately preceding representation account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory demand identifies the substrate, representational origin, predictive machinery, and boundary questions with stable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames the point as an unresolved explanatory demand and openly states uncertainty rather than claiming disproof.

charity.alternative: The pro account presently establishes ontological compatibility, leaving detailed predictive mechanisms to empirical science.
charity.decisiveQualification: Compatibility does not yet answer why the proposed substrate yields boundaries and predictive representational organization.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The demand follows directly from the difference between renaming a substrate and explaining its structured representational behavior.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Predictive processing supplies a concrete explanatory benchmark, though the move does not establish that idealism cannot eventually meet it.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con route's central explanatory-demand bridge concerning machinery, boundaries, and predictive representations.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge allows that both parties may be representationalists but accurately isolates what the ontological label leaves unexplained.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks why brains are prediction machines, how mentality helps explain this, and where the representations and their substrate originate.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Dissociative boundaries can appear as embodied sensory interfaces, while natural selection and stable non-deliberative dispositions account for biological differentiation, causal regularity, and physical predictability.
moves.attributionBasis: The response identifies bodily surfaces as dissociative boundaries and continues Kastrup's characteristic analytic-idealist explanation without a speaker change.

components.text: The decisive demand is to account for boundaries, biological differentiation, and stable predictive order under idealism.

response.rationale: The response identifies bodily interfaces as appearances of dissociative boundaries and invokes reproduction, selection, and stable dispositions to explain differentiation and regularity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive demand but only partly explains why dissociation and stable dispositions have the specified structure.

precisionFindings.rationale: The overall account is recoverable, but dissociation shifts between a process, boundary, and explanatory analogy without full specification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speculative origin claim is candidly qualified, although natural selection presupposes rather than fully grounds the relevant regularities.

charity.alternative: Predictive organization and bodily boundaries require more than an analogy to psychological dissociation and appeal to selection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Selection can explain retained biological forms only after reproducible variation and stable causal rules are available.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The story is mutually compatible, but the bridge from universal mentality to dissociation and preselection regularity remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Embodied boundaries and selection offer illustrative support, while the ontological mapping and intrinsic dispositions remain substantially asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central objectivity bridge by addressing embodied boundaries, evolution, and predictable worldly behavior.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response addresses the strongest mechanistic concern but does not fully absorb the qualification about antecedent causal order.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies skin and sensory surfaces with dissociative boundaries, then invokes reproducible dissociation and natural selection to explain differentiation.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Neutral monism can avoid the hard problem by locating what-it-is-like in a bat's representation rather than moving from experience to a separately presumed physical bat.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly states her own view, develops Nagel's bat example, and asks Bernardo for his response at the end.

components.text: The decisive demand is to avoid the hard problem without presuming a physical object that generates experience.
The foundational inference must exclude a neutral representational basis rather than only nonexperiential matter.

response.rationale: The move proposes a neutral representational location for what-it-is-like and thereby directly challenges the inference from the hard problem to consciousness as universal substance.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive emergence issue with a genuine rival, though the neutral basis itself remains underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The bat-representation proposal is clear, but representation and its neutral bearer are not fully distinguished or specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker explicitly presents the view as exploratory rather than established, matching the limited support supplied.

charity.alternative: The pro view locates representation within consciousness and does not infer experience from a separately presumed physical bat.
charity.decisiveQualification: Avoiding a physical bat does not itself show that representations can possess phenomenality without a conscious substrate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The alternative blocks one physicalist inference, but it leaves a material bridge from neutral representation to what-it-is-like.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The bat example illustrates the proposal, while evidence or mechanism establishing phenomenality of representations is not supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion route by offering neutral monism as a putatively sufficient alternative to idealism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies common ground on rejecting physical emergence but leaves the pro concern about representation's phenomenal bearer incompletely answered.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects moving from experience to a presumed physical bat and instead locates what-it-is-like in the bat's representation.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: The enduring personal agent may be a representational self-model, but even an experienced illusion presupposes consciousness, so dissolving the self does not eliminate phenomenality.
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup addresses Blackmore's known view, accepts her self-model analysis, and contrasts its consequences under materialism and idealism.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether representational or illusory self-models can possess phenomenality without presupposing consciousness.

response.rationale: The reply accepts that the enduring self can be a constructed model but argues that experiencing any illusion still requires phenomenality that idealism retains.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the phenomenality issue clearly, though it does not directly refute every neutral account of phenomenal representation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The narrative self, illusion, experience, idealism, and materialist illusionism are kept sufficiently distinct and qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited necessity claim—that an experienced illusion entails experience—is analytic and does not require additional uncertainty.

charity.alternative: A neutral monist may affirm phenomenality while denying both a persistent self and consciousness as universal substance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Refuting eliminative illusionism does not by itself refute a neutral ontology that preserves phenomenal representation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The core inference from experienced illusion to phenomenality is valid, though its extension to idealism over neutral monism is incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction supplies good warrant for preserving experience, but not for uniquely selecting the idealist ontology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary self-model bridge by separating consciousness from the constructed personal agent.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly accepts the self-model thesis but groups the neutral alternative too closely with materialist elimination at its final step.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts a self-delusive model but insists that illusions are still experienced and that an ontology must leave room for that experience.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: If phenomenal character belongs to representations, fleeting models at multiple processing levels may each have something it is like to be them even when the organizing self-model dissolves.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker declines Kastrup's final inference and develops a first-person proposal grounded in predictive hierarchies, meditation, and self-model dissolution.

components.text: The decisive demand is to locate phenomenality after the organizing phenomenal self-model has dissolved.

response.rationale: The reply agrees that self-model dissolution leaves processing and proposes that multiple transient representations themselves each carry what-it-is-like.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the distinction between selfhood and phenomenality, but asserts rather than explains representation-level experience.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposal is recoverable, though which models qualify as representations with phenomenality and at what levels remains unsettled.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Questions and exploratory language appropriately match the speculative proposal about phenomenality across processing levels.

charity.alternative: Consciousness may remain when a narrative self-model dissolves without each lower-level representation becoming a separate phenomenal subject.
charity.decisiveQualification: Selfless experience supports independence from narrative selfhood, not automatically phenomenality of every transient model.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposal is consistent, but the inference from many models to something-it-is-like for each model leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Meditative self-model dissolution supports selfless experience, while it does not independently verify phenomenality at every processing level.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central con representation bridge by locating phenomenal character in transient representations.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move engages the strongest distinction but moves too quickly from abundant processing to distributed phenomenal viewpoints.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes the phenomenal self-model from extensive other processing and asks whether all those models have something it is like to be them.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: On the invoked IIT account, a maximal complex can exclude states to maximize integration while the excluded integrated processes retain subjective viewpoints outside the narrative self.
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup explicitly returns to his theoretical comfort zone and introduces IIT as support for Blackmore's immediately preceding proposal.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether integrated processes outside the narrative self can retain their own subjective viewpoints.

response.rationale: The reply uses IIT's maximal-complex and exclusion ideas to give a structured account under which shed integrated processes retain viewpoints beyond the ego model.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly supports the proposed multiplicity of viewpoints, although this imports IIT's disputed phenomenal postulate.

precisionFindings.rationale: The maximal-complex account is recoverable, but technical terms and the status of excluded complexes are only briefly explained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account speaks assertively about retained viewpoints even though the cited integration structure does not itself establish phenomenality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The internal IIT description is coherent, but the bridge from excluded integrated processes to subjective viewpoints remains materially assumed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: IIT provides a definite structural framework, while its phenomenal interpretation is asserted without empirical or comparative defense here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the con subsidiary integration challenge by offering a proposed link between complexes and viewpoints.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mainly extends the preceding proposal through IIT rather than testing a clearly developed opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes a maximal integrated complex shedding states and says the excluded integrated mental processes retain subjective points of view.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Integrated information theory does not explain why greater information integration entails subjective experience or what it means for consciousness to exist in greater or lesser degree.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly addresses Bernardo and explicitly challenges his preceding account of integrated information theory.

components.text: The decisive demand is why greater integration or a maximal complex entails any subjective point of view.

response.rationale: The reply directly identifies the missing explanatory connection between measured integrated information and what-it-is-like or degrees of consciousness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly targets the decisive inference rather than merely disputing IIT's complexity or empirical usefulness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between integration, its measurement, phenomenal existence, and degrees of consciousness is sharply recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The challenge is framed as a request for clarification and candidly acknowledges limited understanding of the technical theory.

charity.alternative: IIT may offer an identity or axiomatic bridge rather than a conventional causal derivation from information to experience.
charity.decisiveQualification: An identity postulate still requires defense of why the formal quantity corresponds to phenomenal existence and degree.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explanatory demand precisely exposes the unsupported transition from integration magnitude to phenomenality and its alleged degree.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The criticism is grounded in the stated IIT claims, though it does not examine a full axiomatic defense of the theory.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It maximally supports the subsidiary integration bridge by directly testing the theory's connection to subjective experience.

representationalCharity.rationale: The question does not reduce IIT to mere correlation and accurately asks for the theory's deepest phenomenal warrant.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks why integrated information yields anything it is like to be and what greater or lesser consciousness could mean.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: IIT's deeper causal account leans toward idealism insofar as self-existing experiential complexes, rather than merely represented objects, possess causal structure and power.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo continues his answer by explicitly shifting from IIT's operational role to its limited ontological implications.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether IIT provides more than correlation by grounding phenomenality in self-existing causal structure.

response.rationale: The response identifies IIT's predictive bridge and deeper causal-existence commitments, while expressly limiting the conclusion to leaning toward rather than implying idealism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the ontological side of the demand but only partly answers why causal structure entails phenomenal character.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited idealist implication is clear, though minimum complexes, ontological dust, and existence-for-itself remain compressed technical notions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The explicit statement that IIT leans toward but does not imply idealism appropriately limits the ontological inference.

charity.alternative: IIT's causal structures could be interpreted realistically without identifying their intrinsic existence with universal consciousness.
charity.decisiveQualification: Existence-for-itself may suggest experience but does not uniquely establish analytic idealism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cautious conclusion follows as a suggested affinity, but the bridge from causal self-existence to experience remains implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stated IIT architecture supports a limited interpretive leaning, while no serious comparison of realist interpretations is developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially attacks the subsidiary integration challenge by supplying a deeper causal and ontological interpretation of IIT.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves this limitation explicitly and avoids treating IIT as a deductive proof of the pro ontology.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes IIT's predictive bridge from its deeper causal structures and expressly says these lean toward but do not imply idealism.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Treating a dreaming subject as the cause of an imagined object is problematic when the causal first-person self invoked by that account lacks clear or stable existence.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan explicitly picks up Bernardo's dream example and interrogates the identity of the purported causal subject.

components.text: The decisive demand is to identify the self-existing subject that supposedly possesses causal power in the dream analogy.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the shift from denying stable selves to saying an I causes the dream object and requests identification of the causal subject.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the causal-agent premise on which the immediately preceding dream illustration depends.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alleged causal I, imagined elephant, and previously disputed self are clearly identified in the challenge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asks for clarification of an apparent tension and does not overstate that tension as a decisive contradiction.

charity.alternative: The causal subject may be consciousness or an experiencing system rather than the narrative autobiographical self.
charity.decisiveQualification: The dream example must distinguish that underlying subject from the self-model previously denied stable existence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The demand follows directly from the ambiguity between an enduring causal subject and a constructed personal self.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The prior agreement about self-model instability supports the tension, though it does not preclude every thinner notion of subject.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro central causal-order bridge by asking what entity carries causal power in the example.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge leaves room for a nonnarrative subject while correctly requiring the causal referent to be made explicit.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt notes the agreed problems with selves and asks what the causal 'you' means when the dream elephant lacks causal power of itself.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Particular experiences are excitations or behaviors of a single core subjectivity, rather than contents produced by separate individual material subjects.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo answers Susan's causal question, marks the transition to his own philosophy, and states his universal-subjectivity view.

components.text: The decisive demand is to identify a causal subject without reinstating the unstable narrative personal self.

response.rationale: The response distinguishes particular experiences as behaviors of a single core subjectivity from a separate personal agent or produced experiential content.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly supplies a nonnarrative subject, though individuation and causal operation remain only partly explained.

precisionFindings.rationale: The excitation-versus-core distinction is recoverable, but metaphors for the dative of experience do not fully stabilize its properties.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The universal core is asserted as the explanatory subject despite the excerpt supplying mainly conceptual distinctions and metaphors.

charity.alternative: A subject may be only a locally integrated process rather than one universal bearer underlying all experiences.
charity.decisiveQualification: Distinguishing experience from its dative does not establish that every dative is numerically one universal subject.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction avoids identifying subjectivity with the narrative self, but numerical unity of the underlying subject remains a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dancer and ripple analogies clarify the claim but do not independently support a single universal core subjectivity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the pro central causal-order bridge by locating experiences in an underlying nonpersonal subject.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply answers the narrative-self objection but gives insufficient attention to the strongest local-process alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes experiences as behaviors or excitations of subjectivity from the core dative to which experiences are given.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Ordinary dreams without an experienced self leave idealism and integrated-information accounts without a clear explanation of what causes one dream element rather than another.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan resumes the dream example and explicitly asks both IIT and analytic idealism to locate the relevant causal factors.

components.text: The decisive demand is to explain differentiated dream events when no experienced personal self directs or causes them.

response.rationale: The reply accepts selfless dreaming as a test case and asks both IIT and idealism to locate the causal factors differentiating one dream element from another.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly tests the proposed core subject against a concrete case lacking an experienced personal agent.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ordinary nonlucid dream case, absent experienced self, differentiated content, and causal demand are clearly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents a concrete unresolved problem and asks how either theory helps, without claiming the case disproves them.

charity.alternative: Universal subjectivity need not contain an experienced personal self to instantiate intrinsic causal dynamics producing dream contents.
charity.decisiveQualification: That possibility still owes an account of why its dynamics produce this differentiated content rather than another.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The challenge validly separates existence of experience from the further explanation of differentiated causal content.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary selfless dreams provide a relevant counterexample to personal-agent language, though not to impersonal causal dynamics.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro central causal-order bridge by demanding differentiation without a personal causal agent.

representationalCharity.rationale: The question preserves the distinction between universal subjectivity and personal selfhood while maintaining the causal-differentiation demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes a remembered nonlucid dream without a real experienced self and asks what causal factors IIT or idealism identifies.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Causal differentiation and complex natural order arise from the intrinsic properties, characteristic excitation modes, harmonics, and self-interference of the one universal field of subjectivity.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo directly answers the causality question by laying out analytic idealism's single-field ontology and its intrinsic properties.

components.text: The decisive demand is to explain differentiated causal order without appeal to a directing personal self.

response.rationale: The reply locates differentiation in intrinsic field properties, characteristic modes, harmonics, and self-interference rather than in deliberate personal agency.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly supplies an impersonal causal scheme, while the asserted intrinsic properties remain unexplained primitives.

precisionFindings.rationale: The field-dynamics proposal is recoverable, though archetypes, excitation modes, and literal versus analogical interference remain partly unsettled.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Simple-rule complexity is plausible, but the analogy does not fully warrant attributing the required modes to universal subjectivity.

charity.alternative: Invoking intrinsic laws and field dynamics may reproduce the structural primitives that idealism criticized in physical accounts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Making the primitives experiential can address intrinsic nature, but it does not by itself explain their particular lawful form.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Intrinsic modes and self-interference can coherently yield complexity, but their connection to subjectivity and particular laws is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Wave interference and simple-rule complexity offer useful analogies, while the universal mental field's specified dynamics remain speculative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the indispensable central causal-order bridge with an impersonal account of differentiation and regularity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response gives a substantive causal model but only partly addresses the concern that its ordering principles are relabeled primitives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt attributes complexity to intrinsic properties, natural frequencies, harmonics, and constructive or destructive self-interference of the one field.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Meditative states in which experience continues without ordinary spatial or temporal organization provide reason to question whether space and time are fundamental.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan frames the issue as a final substantive question and grounds it in her extensive first-person meditation experience.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether the field account requires ordinary spatial and temporal organization to explain experience.

response.rationale: The move introduces continued experience without ordinary spatial or temporal organization as evidence bearing on what the proposed fundamental structure must explain.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It raises a relevant structural test but does not directly analyze the preceding excitation and self-interference mechanism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is clear, though the phenomenological absence of ordinary organization and metaphysical nonfundamentality are not fully separated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The experience is offered as a reason to question fundamentality, not as certain proof that space and time are absent ontologically.

charity.alternative: Altered experience may cease representing space and time even if underlying causal processes remain spatially and temporally organized.
charity.decisiveQualification: Phenomenological absence alone does not establish ontological absence, but it constrains claims that such organization is essential to experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The phenomenological observation supports questioning fundamentality, provided the inference remains explicitly defeasible as presented.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Extensive first-person meditation supplies relevant experiential evidence, but its ontological interpretation requires independent verification and rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary altered-experience bridge by testing whether ordinary spacetime organization is necessary.

representationalCharity.rationale: The cautious framing accommodates the representational alternative while preserving the experience's legitimate evidential relevance.
